title: Al-Layl: the night
hookLine: by the night and the day, your strivings are different (Surah 92)

lines: TWO PEOPLE, THE SAME DARK STREET.
cards: Eleven at night, one quiet street, two people under the same streetlight. One is driving home from a double shift so her kids can eat. The other is out to do something he hopes nobody finds out about.
From a satellite, they look identical: two dots moving in the dark. The night covers them both. What's different is where each one is going, and why.

The surah just before Ad-Duha, Al-Layl, the night, opens on that same picture: night and day, male and female, and then a sentence that could be written about any street, any office, any family group chat.

teach.b: Surah ninety-two begins, in Pickthall's translation: By the night enshrouding. The night that covers, that wraps things so you can't see them.
Then by the day when it shines, and by the One who created the male and the female. Three oaths, all pairs: dark and light, one and the other.
Then the point they lead to, verse four, in Pickthall's words: Lo! your effort is dispersed. Scattered, going in different directions.

The Arabic word for effort is sa'y, effort with your feet in it, hurrying toward something. Pilgrims use the same word, sa'y, for the walk between the hills of Safa and Marwa during Hajj, retracing Hajar's run for water.

And shatta, the word describing the effort, means scattered, as different from each other as night from day. So: everyone is under the same sky, but the efforts aren't the same. Some run toward what's good.
Some run away from it. The night hides the difference for a while. It doesn't erase it.
Notice what the surah doesn't say: not that effort is wasted, or that effort is bad.
Only that effort has a direction. The next verses, tomorrow's, name the two directions; today is only the question.
It's the end of a week, too: At-Tin, made in the best form; Ash-Sharh, the chest opened and hardship paired with ease; Ad-Duha, the morning, the orphan and the gift told out loud.
Now the night, and the question under all of them: where is the effort going?

how: Al-Layl is one of the short surahs often learned by heart and recited in the prayer; its opening oaths, by the night and the day, are often read as a reminder that every person's effort is heading somewhere.

o: the rising sun, and the surah that swears by it
the evening prayer said just after sunset
the night, and the surah that swears by it

games.q: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.
p: the walk called sa'y in Hajj

s: Surah 92 says all human effort is wasted
it says efforts differ: they go in different directions, not that they're pointless.
the opening oaths of Al-Layl come in pairs
night and day, male and female: opposites, before the line about differing efforts.
the walk between Safa and Marwa is also called sa'y
the same word as the effort in 92:4: hurrying, striving toward something.

games.q: Al-Layl swears by the night, the day, and the creation of male and female. what does it say next?
o: that night is better than day
that the world will end at night
games.why: your striving is scattered, going in different directions. the oaths in pairs set up the point: same sky, different directions.

practice: Look back over yesterday as if from above, like that satellite, and ask where your effort actually went, not where you meant it to go: the phone, the work, a person, a worry. Don't judge it.
Just notice the direction, the way you'd notice which way a river runs.

wordCard.voice: Al-Layl. The night, the name of Surah ninety-two, which swears by the night and the day and says your efforts differ. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the night, the name of Surah 92, which opens by swearing by the night as it covers.

carryVoice: Your line: efforts differ. Same sky, same night, and the roads still part. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:158 (Safa and Marwa); Sahih al-Bukhari 3364 (Hajar's search for water)
